lead: A beam is a bar that carries loads sideways on its axis, so it bends. Before drawing a shear force diagram, replace the real bridge, slab or machine part by a model: a line for the beam, standard supports, standard loads. The model gives the number of unknown reactions and shows whether the three equilibrium equations can find them.
prereq: Force, moment of a force about a point, and equilibrium of a rigid body from first-year mechanics.

sections.h3: Beam, span and what the model assumes

blocks.text: A beam is a bar whose length far exceeds its cross-section, carrying loads transverse — sideways — to its axis. Slabs, girders, rails, axles and machine beds are analysed as beams.

The span is the distance between two supports; on a cantilever, from the support to the free end. The effective span is measured between bearing centres: a 5 m clear gap with 200 mm bearings each side gives 5.2 m.
Five assumptions turn the real member into a line model:

items: The beam is its own straight axis; thickness and shape matter later, for stress (see Unit 4, Bending and Shear Stresses in Beams).
All loads act in one plane through the axis, so the beam bends in that plane only.
Deflections are small compared with the span.
Plane sections stay plane after bending.
Self weight is neglected or added as a uniformly distributed load.

sections.h3: Supports: count the movements they stop

blocks.text: A support stops some movements of the beam end and allows the rest. Each stopped movement brings a reaction, so count the movements prevented to get the number of unknowns.
Pin (hinge). Stops sliding in any direction in the plane, allows rotation. Two reactions: H horizontal and V vertical, in kN. A door hinge behaves like this.
Roller. Stops movement normal (perpendicular) to its surface; allows sliding along it and rotation. One reaction V, normal to the surface. On a slope it is not vertical, so resolve it into parts.
Fixed (built-in). Stops translation and rotation. Three reactions: H, V and a moment M in kN·m. A steel beam cast into a concrete wall is the usual picture.
Watch the words: some syllabi say simple support for a roller or knife edge, and simply supported beam for a pin at one end and a roller at the other. Read the term from the sketch.
A point load is a force at one section, in kN. In reality it acts over a small area — a wheel on a rail — small against the span, so we draw an arrow.

A uniformly distributed load (UDL) has intensity w in kN/m over length L. Its total acts at the middle of the loaded length, not the middle of the whole beam when the load covers part of the span. Self weight is a UDL: w = ρ A g / 1000 in kN/m, with ρ the density in kg/m³, A the cross-section area in m² and g = 9.81 m/s².

blocks.where: W is the total of a UDL in kN; w is its intensity in kN/m; L is the loaded length in m; x̄ is the distance from the start of the load to the line of action of W, in m.

blocks.text: A uniformly varying load (UVL) rises linearly from zero to w over length L. Its total is ½ w L, acting at 2L/3 from the zero end — the centroid of a triangle. Split a trapezoidal load into a rectangle plus a triangle.
An applied couple is a pure moment M in kN·m — a shaft keyed into a beam. An eccentric load becomes a concentric force plus a couple; only the couple part is the applied moment.
Units carry the meaning: kN per metre of length, not per square metre. A slab pressure p in kN/m² on a strip b metres wide becomes w = p b kN/m.

items: Cantilever: fixed at one end, free at the other.
Simply supported: pin at one end, roller at the other.
Overhanging: two supports, the beam running past one or both (see 3.4).
Propped cantilever: fixed at one end, a roller prop at the other.
Continuous: more than two supports, such as a pipeline over several piers.

blocks.text: A plane beam gives three equilibrium equations: ΣH = 0, ΣV = 0 and ΣM = 0. Count the unknown reactions r. If r = 3 the beam is statically determinate — equilibrium alone finds every reaction. If r > 3 it is statically indeterminate of degree r − 3, and compatibility of deflections is needed (see Unit 5, Deflection of Beams and Energy Methods).
Quick count: simply supported 2 + 1 = 3; propped cantilever 4, degree 1; fixed-fixed 6, degree 3. A cantilever's single fixed end gives three unknowns — exactly three equations, so determinate.
Sign convention: sagging is positive. A bending moment that curves the beam concave up — tension at the bottom fibre — is positive; hogging, concave down, is negative.

figure.caption: The beam model has two halves: supports, which give the unknown reactions you must find, and loads, which are known. Notice that only the fixed support brings a moment as well as forces.

spec.aria: A beam model splits into three support types with their reaction counts and four load types with their totals.

examples.question: A beam AB is 6 m long, pinned at A and on a roller at B at the right end. It carries a 20 kN point load 2 m from A and a uniformly distributed load of 5 kN/m over the whole span. (a) Name the beam. (b) List every unknown reaction. (c) State the total of the UDL and where it acts. (d) Say whether the beam is statically determinate.
steps: Pin at A gives H<sub>A</sub> and V<sub>A</sub>; the roller at B gives V<sub>B</sub>, vertical. Unknowns r = 2 + 1 = 3.
One pin and one roller at the ends, span 6 m, no overhang: a simply supported beam.
UDL: W = w × L = 5 × 6 = 30 kN, acting at x̄ = L / 2 = 6 / 2 = 3 m from A.
The 20 kN point load at 2 m from A adds loading but no unknown.
Plane equilibrium gives three equations: ΣH = 0, ΣV = 0, ΣM = 0.
r − 3 = 3 − 3 = 0, so the beam is statically determinate. The reaction arithmetic is in 3.2.
examples.answer: Simply supported beam; unknowns H<sub>A</sub>, V<sub>A</sub> and V<sub>B</sub> — three against three equilibrium equations; the UDL totals 30 kN at 3 m from A; degree 0, determinate.
examples.check:
L = 6.0      # span, m
w = 5.0      # UDL intensity, kN/m
P = 20.0     # point load, kN
a = 2.0      # point load position from A, m

W = w * L          # total UDL, kN
print(W)
print(L / 2)       # where the UDL acts, m from A
r = 2 + 1          # pin gives 2, roller gives 1
print(r)
eq = 3             # plane equilibrium equations
print(eq)
print(r - eq)      # degree of indeterminacy

traps: Treating a roller as a pin invents a horizontal reaction. A roller gives one reaction, normal to its surface; on a slope that reaction is not vertical.
The total of a UDL is w × L, not w, and it acts at the middle of the loaded length, not of the span when the load is partial.
Unit slips: w in kN/m times L in m gives kN; a slab pressure in kN/m² needs the strip width to become kN/m; a moment is in kN·m only when force is in kN and length in m.
Forgetting the moment reaction at a fixed end makes a fixed or propped beam look determinate. A fixed support always contributes three unknowns.
A simply supported beam needs a pin plus a roller; a simple support is one device. Draw the roller with its gap or circles.

quiz.q: Define a beam and its span.
quiz.a: A bar whose length far exceeds its cross-section, carrying loads transverse to its axis. Span is the distance between supports; on a cantilever, support to free end.

quiz.q: How many reactions does a roller give, and in which direction?
quiz.a: One, acting normal (perpendicular) to the surface it rests on. On a horizontal floor it is vertical.

quiz.q: Why does a pin give two reactions but a roller only one?
quiz.a: A reaction appears for each movement prevented. A pin prevents sliding in both plane directions but allows rotation, so H and V. A roller prevents movement only normal to its surface, so one reaction.

quiz.q: Why is the self weight of a beam drawn as a UDL?
quiz.a: The weight is spread evenly along the length: each metre carries ρ A g newtons, so w = ρ A g / 1000 kN/m, constant along the span.

quiz.q: A simply supported beam of span 8 m carries a UDL of 12 kN/m over its whole span. Find the total load and where it acts.
quiz.a: W = w × L = 12 × 8 = 96 kN, acting at L/2 = 4 m from either support.

quiz.q: A beam of span 6 m carries a UVL that is zero at A and 15 kN/m at B. Find the total load and its line of action.
quiz.a: W = ½ w L = ½ × 15 × 6 = 45 kN, acting at 2L/3 = 4 m from A (the zero end), that is 2 m from B.

quiz.q: A beam is fixed at A and rests on a roller at B. How many unknown reactions are there, and is the beam determinate?
quiz.a: Fixed end gives H<sub>A</sub>, V<sub>A</sub>, M<sub>A</sub> = 3; roller gives V<sub>B</sub> = 1. Total 4 against 3 equations, so it is statically indeterminate of degree 1 — a propped cantilever. Deflection compatibility finds the fourth reaction.

quiz.q: A 5 m beam is pinned at A and on a roller at B, carrying a 10 kN point load at mid-span and a UDL of 4 kN/m over the whole span. A student replaces the roller by a fixed support. State what changes in the unknown count and in the degree of indeterminacy.
quiz.a: Original: 2 + 1 = 3 unknowns, degree 0, determinate. With a fixed end at B: 2 + 3 = 5 unknowns, degree 5 − 3 = 2. The loads are unchanged (UDL total 4 × 5 = 20 kN at 2.5 m), but two extra unknowns appear — a horizontal reaction and a moment at B — that equilibrium alone cannot give.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real bearings — steel rollers, elastomeric pads, pot bearings — carry a moment as well as a force, and soil settlement moves a support. Influence lines show where to place a moving truck for the worst shear or moment. Finite element models replace each support by a spring stiffness.
